newsitem.title: CUBA: Small explosion damages Havana hotel-witnesses.
newsitem.headline: Small explosion damages Havana hotel-witnesses.

text.p: A small explosion, possibly caused by a bomb or firework, damaged the lobby of central Havana's top hotel early on Monday, witnesses said.

Dutch tourist Roberto Koppens told reporters he arrived in the lobby of the Melia Cohiba hotel several minutes after an explosion and saw smoke, minor damage to furnishings, and could smell gunpowder.
The explosion at the Cohiba came just three weeks after two bombs rocked the lobbies of two other Havana hotels, the Nacional and the Capri, causing damage and slightly injuring three people.

Officials at the Cohiba, which is owned by the Cuban state firm Cubanacan and managed by Spanish hotel chain Sol Melia, declined to comment on the incident, which occurred at about 7:30 a.m. (1130 GMT).

The director of Cubanacan, Juan Jose de la Vega, visited the hotel during the morning but declined to confirm there had been a bomb or firecracker. Pressed by reporters outside the hotel to comment, he said "it was a lot of noise." He said nobody was injured.
Part of the lobby of the highrise hotel was sealed off with a wooden partition and workmen could be heard hammering. It was not possible to see the damage behind the screen.
Several uniformed and plain clothes security officials milled around the lobby, preventing people who were not guests from entering the hotel. A guard dog patroled behind the wooden partition.
Wooden boards were also mounted along the outside of one smoked glass side of the lobby, but it was not possible to see if any windows were broken.
The explosion coincided with an international leftist youth festival which concludes on Tuesday and which has drawn more than 10,000 young people from around the world to the Cuban capital.
Most of the delegates at the nine-day festival of discussion groups and concerts are staying in private Cuban families or at cheaper hotels in the city.

Dutch tourist Koppens said that although he had not heard the explosion from his room high in the hotel tower, he arrived in the lobby just minutes later. He said he had spoken with another tourist who he said heard a loud bang.
Koppens said he believed there were no injuries, but said hotel workers at the reception desk area were clearly alarmed. Sources at the hotel said the explosion was not serious.
The small bombs three weeks ago exploded during the morning of July 12 and were seen and heard by so many guests and passers-by that it was impossible to conceal them.
At the time, the Cuban Interior Ministry issued a brief statement saying it had evidence that the people involved and the materials used in the bombs came from the United States.
The U.S. State Department has said that Havana should produce evidence or stop making the accusation.

The Melia Cohiba, situated on Havana's Malecon sea-front drive in Vedado district, was also allegedly the target of a small bomb in April. Officials from the Sol Melia chain acknowledged at the time that there had been an explosion, but that it was caused by faulty gas piping.
Cuba is extremely anxious to preserve its image as a safe place to visit as it seeks to encourage the growth of tourism.
